identity: An Arabic children's cartoon/anime theme song (نشيد المقدمة), informally transcribed one sung line per line: 21 lines of 2-4 tokens each, 93 tokens total. Register markers are unmistakable: strict end-rhyme (الكوكب/نركب, نتحدى/نهدى, كالأطفال/كالأبطال, نبقى/نرقى, أنقى/أمضى), first-person-plural heroic address (نمضي نتحرى نتحدى نصد الشر), and a verse-then-chorus structure in which lines 14-21 are a near-verbatim repeat of lines 3, 4, 6 and 8. It is a fan/amateur transcription, not an edited text: تيالي for تبالي, بضلم for بظلم, نضل for نظل, and the same rhyme-words spelled inconsistently with alif or alif maqsura across repetitions (نرقا @33 vs نرقى @73/@92; نهدى @16 vs نهدا @63/@82; نتحدى @11/@77 vs نتحدا @58). Such a source carries no sentence punctuation at all - the transcriber marked the song by breaking lines, nothing else.
law: THE UNIT IS THE LYRIC LINE. One layout slot, one segment - the same law as a comic balloon (doctrine §T), an MCQ option (§S), a worksheet cell (§J). Because this transcription has no internal punctuation of its own, its only sentence-final marks in the source are the line breaks themselves, and LAW 0' says a boundary is a sentence-final OR LAYOUT-final mark and nothing else. Therefore the boundary set is exactly the 21 line-final tokens and contains nothing else. The proof that the segmentation is typographic rather than syntactic is line 10: بالخوف و بضلم الأشرار is a bare prepositional phrase governed by the imperative تيالي that ends line 9 - the line break severs a verb from its own complement and is still a boundary. If the annotators cut through a verb-complement joint on ink alone, then a fortiori no site INSIDE a 2-4 token line can be cut, since no ink falls there. Line length here (2-4 tokens) is the shortest in the corpus, well under the worksheet range of §J, and it is 100 percent coincident with <NL>: 21 lines, 21 boundaries, zero internal.
reasoning: FIRST, the register call, because doctrine's Step Zero says identify the unit system before placing any boundary. This is not prose, so the printed-full-stop default does not apply; it is a layout register, and the layout slot is the sung line. Doctrine's best-scoring documents (worksheets at F1 99.3/99.2, comic strips at 94.3) are exactly this shape, and my worst failures in batch 2 all came from importing a syntactic cut-reflex into a layout register. SECOND, the hard sites, all of which are candidates for ADDING a cut inside a line, and all of which I resolve as WELD. (1) The asyndetic verb triples نمضي نتحرى نتحدى @9-11, @56-58, @75-77, and نمضي بسفينتنا نركب @5-7. Batch-1 LAW 3 would have cut these as parallel repetition; batch 2 killed that discriminator and replaced it with the question 'was each element a complete PRINTED sentence, or an item inside one?' In an unpunctuated lyric transcription nothing inside a line is a printed sentence - at most these would have carried commas, and a comma is not a boundary; that single clause caused roughly 300 of my 354 false cuts in batch 2. Weld. This is also the §P1 pattern, where gold grouped short asyndetic clauses two-and-two rather than one-per-clause, and I lost 38 cuts by splitting them. (2) هيا @35. This is my one genuine hesitation, because H3 (bare interjection is its own segment) is my most reliable positive cue outside <NL> and accounted for 5 of my 16 batch-2 misses. I weld it, on three grounds: H3's cutting cases were all conversational TURNS - حسنا answered by an imperative in a new balloon, مولاي and يا أمير المؤمنين opening a speech - whereas هيا here is proclitic to the imperative it introduces, forming one exhortation هيا لا تبالي بالخوف وبظلم الأشرار that in fact spans two lines; §T-1 explicitly welds an interjection to its statement inside one balloon (يا إلهي لا أستطيع منح الجائزة), and §U @28 welds نعم يا سيدي to what follows; and cutting after هيا would isolate a single token inside a three-token line, which no layout mark supports. Weld. (3) The و-joints: ولا نهدى @15, و بضلم @40, و السيف @47, و دوما @65 and @84. LAW 1 as revised is unambiguous - و is never by itself a reason to cut, and in batch 2 it was my single largest false-cut class even where it introduced a brand-new subject with its own nominal predicate. و السيف أمضي is precisely that shape (new subject, nominal predicate, parallel to فالحق أنقى) and it needs no decision from me anyway, since the line break at أنقى @45 already supplies the boundary. Weld. (4) لكنا @22. B4 as revised: a لكن-clause welds by default at any length and cuts only after an end-stop; here it is a whole line and the boundary is already given at نبقى @24. Weld. (5) فالحق @44. LAW 2 as revised: ف is a continuation marker and counts slightly AGAINST cutting; the boundary before it comes from the line break at تيالي... in fact from الأشرار @42, not from the ف. Weld. THIRD, I considered whether the unit could be the rhyming COUPLET rather than the line, which would give fewer boundaries than lines; the task statement forecloses this by guaranteeing that the mark before every <NL> is correct, so the couplet reading is excluded and the line reading is confirmed. FOURTH, the arithmetic check on my own bias: I am proposing 21 boundaries for 21 lines and zero discretionary cuts. Given that batch 2 ran 22:1 over-cutting and that every discretionary cue available in this document (asyndeton, و, ف, لكن, interjection) is on doctrine's explicit do-not-cut list, a zero-addition answer is the calibrated one. The document is effectively a free document; my only way to lose points here is to invent a cut, so I invent none.
